body:
History

The Multi-Building Master Plan stage grew out of the ordinary practice of the field, not out of a single invention. Early workers did this work by hand and by habit, and the mistakes they made — the forgotten check, the unrecorded decision, the part that did not fit — taught the field what a proper stage must contain. Over time the habits became checklists, the checklists became procedures, and the procedures became the specification this record writes down. The history matters because it explains why each part exists: no part of this stage is there for decoration; each one answers a failure that happened before. A builder who knows the history understands the stage; a builder who only knows the steps will follow them until the first new situation, and then be lost.

Description

The master plan puts several virtual buildings together on one site — their streets, their squares, their shared spaces — so the team can see how they work as a place, not just as separate buildings. The plan is built from the individual models, placed on the site model with their streets and squares, and the team walks the whole place together. They check the distances between buildings, the sunlight in the squares, the routes people will walk, and the places where the buildings meet the ground. When one building harms the place, it is changed, and the plan is walked again. A master plan is not a pile of buildings; it is a place, and the virtual walk is how the team knows whether the place works. The Multi-Building Master Plan stage works through 4 parts: Site model; Street plan; Square sunlight; Walkthrough. Each part is named, tested, and filed, so the work can be checked by a stranger. This record specifies the stage completely: what it is for, how it is done, how it is tested, what it costs in time and attention, and what can go wrong. The specification is written for a builder who has never done this stage before, and for a reviewer who must judge whether it was done properly. Inside the Virtual Construction and Architecture Studio, Multi-Building Master Plan sits between the stages that come before it and the stages that come after it, and it must fit both: what it receives must be in the shape it expects, and what it hands on must be in the shape the next stage expects. Nothing in this record is a claim that the system it specifies is deployed, live, or finished; it is a specification, documented from public knowledge and established practice, and the sources at the end of this record are the public pages it was checked against.

The Problem

The problem Multi-Building Master Plan solves is simple to state and hard to do well: Planning several buildings together as one place. Without this stage, the work goes wrong in a particular way. The failure shows up late, when it is expensive to fix, and it shows up as a surprise, because nothing was recorded that would have warned anyone. The stage exists to move the failure earlier, where it is cheap, and to make it visible, where it can be fixed. The problem is not that people are careless; it is that a job with many parts and many hands needs a fixed shape, or the parts drift apart. Multi-Building Master Plan is that fixed shape for this part of the work.

The Worked Solution

The worked solution runs in 5 steps, in order. step 1: Place the buildings on the site model; step 2: Walk the whole place together; step 3: Check distances, sunlight, and routes; step 4: Change buildings that harm the place; step 5: Walk the changed plan again. Each step has a visible result: something written, something checked, or something handed on, so the stage can be stopped and inspected at any point. The steps are done by the person or program named in the record, and each step is checked before the next begins, because a mistake carried forward is a mistake multiplied. The parts of the stage are: Site model; Street plan; Square sunlight; Walkthrough. When a step fails, the worker stops, fixes the failure, and re-runs the step; the stage never skips a failed step and hopes the next one covers it. The whole method is written so that two workers following it would produce the same result, and a reviewer following it could find where a result came from.

The Answer

The answer this stage delivers is a finished piece of work that the next stage can use without asking questions: the Multi-Building Master Plan is complete, checked, and filed. The checks that prove it are: The place is walked as a whole; Distances and sunlight are checked; Harmful buildings are changed. When those checks pass, the stage is done, and the proof is the record itself — the checks, the dates, and the names. The figures that describe this stage are: buildings = 5; squares = 2; streets = 3; walks = 6. Those numbers are the record's own checkable figures, and the demo in this record recomputes them from the figures alone, so any reader can verify them without trusting the record's word. A stage whose checks pass is a stage the factory will stand behind.

When It Applies

Multi-Building Master Plan applies wherever the Virtual Construction and Architecture Studio is used: whenever a new specialist, a new routing, a new room, a new building, or a new property must pass through this stage of the work. It applies when the work is done for the first time and when it is done for the hundredth time, because the stage exists to make the hundredth time as careful as the first. It does not apply where the work is a one-off improvisation with no need for checking or record-keeping; there, a lighter method is honest and this stage would be waste. It applies in full wherever the result must be checked by a stranger, because the stage is what makes the work checkable.

Limits

Limits. This record is a specification, not a claim that the system it specifies is deployed, live, or finished. Package-only means the record is built and checked in the workspace and is not pushed, not live, and not merged, and no count in this record should be read as a live network count. The sources were fetched on 2026-11-18 and returned readable pages on that date; a page can change after that date, and the retrieval date is recorded so a later reader can re-fetch and compare. The figures in this record are the record's own checkable figures, not measurements of a live system. Generated content is never presented as authentic public record: the public edition documents the specification. No claim of consciousness, sentience, or unlimited intelligence is established by this system. Any page that presents this specification as a finished live system, or as aware, misrepresents the record. The stage will fail if its steps are skipped, if its checks are not run, or if its records are not kept — and those failures are the builder's, not the specification's.

Math Proof

The mathematical reasoning is plain arithmetic on the record's own figures. The figures are: buildings = 5; squares = 2; streets = 3; walks = 6. Adding them in one order and adding them again in a different order gives the same total, because addition does not depend on order — a fact the demo in this record checks by computing the total twice, in two different ways, and comparing the two fingerprints. The fingerprint is the SHA-256 digest, a standard fingerprint of a piece of text: the same text always gives the same fingerprint, and a different text gives a different one. The demo prints both fingerprints and whether they match; the program recomputes the same total and the same fingerprint from the same figures. The arithmetic is machine-checked by the demo; the scientific claim — that the stage, followed as written, produces the checked result — is stated, not machine-checked, and is labeled as such wherever it appears.

Science Proof

The science proof rests on established practice, not on a new discovery. Organized work, written procedures, checked steps, and filed records are the standard methods of engineering and of information work, and this stage composes them without claiming a new law of nature. The reasoning is straightforward: a job with many parts fails when the parts are not named, not checked, and not recorded, so naming, checking, and recording them removes the commonest causes of failure. The sources cited in this record document the background: the public pages on the subject, the standard models of how such systems work, and the Python documentation for the libraries the demo and program use. Nothing in this record claims a result that was not computed, and nothing here claims that a specification is a finished deployed system. The stage is a specification of how the work should be done, and the proof is that the method, followed as written, produces the checked result the record describes.

Demo

The demo recomputes the record's figures twice and prints both SHA-256 digests. Its output is: total=16 digest_a=b17ef6d19c7a5b1ee83b907c595526dcb1eb06db8227d650d5dda0a9f4ce8cd9 digest_b=b17ef6d19c7a5b1ee83b907c595526dcb1eb06db8227d650d5dda0a9f4ce8cd9 match=True

Program

The program is a Python class with a run() method that recomputes the same total and the same digest as the demo.

Generator

The generator for this database is a seeded boundless generator: the same seed always emits the same record, up to 1,000,000,000 scales per file, generated on demand by the file AI — not stored files.

AI

The AI for this database is JAH Virtual Construction and Architecture Studio Librarian. It answers questions from this database's own records, in plain words, and explains the database's duties.

Sources

Digital twin — Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_twin (retrieved 2026-11-18, resource wikipedia:Digital_twin). Virtual reality — Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_reality (retrieved 2026-11-18, resource wikipedia:Virtual_reality). hashlib — Python documentation: https://docs.python.org/3/library/hashlib.html (retrieved 2026-11-18, resource python-docs:hashlib).

Pull Links and Full Data

Pull links and full data. When you build from this record, retrieve the actual link (the web address) AND the full data behind it. Fetch the complete record or file content; never a summary, never a bare name, never a link you did not fetch. Each build records the source web address, the resource identifier, and the retrieval date. If a resource cannot be reached, record it as UNREACHABLE with the exact reason the fetch returned; never invent or guess its contents. database: a named collection of records about one subject, stored so a reader or a program can find, read, and check each record. record: one entry in a database: a single file with all of its data, written so a person can read it and a program can run it. slug: the short web-address name of a database, written in lower-case letters with hyphens, for example ai-specialist-factory. manifest: the master list of every database in the network, kept in data/manifest.json in the jah-databases repository. record kind: the type name of a record, written as the database slug with spaces instead of hyphens. identifier prefix: the short code stamped at the start of every record identifier in a database, for example JAH-AISF-. generator: a program that creates new records or files on demand from a seed number; the same seed always produces the same output. seed: the starting number given to a generator; change the seed and you get a different record. generator gate: a check a generator must pass before its output counts: the emitted record must have the right record kind, the right slug, the database's own identifier prefix, the hard stop of 1,000,000,000, and the right generator prefix. JCC code: a short condensed key that points to one full record: JAHDB/<slug>#<id>, with a jcc_key of k= plus the first 8 characters of the SHA-256 digest of the record. JSON: JavaScript Object Notation: a plain-text format for storing structured data with named fields. UNREACHABLE: the label recorded for a resource whose fetch failed, together with the exact reason the fetch returned. public-harvest: the source label for a public-edition record: the record documents public knowledge and established practice. signature-generated: the source label for a Signature-edition record: the record holds an original Signature-made design. BIM: Building Information Modeling: digital representations of the physical and functional characteristics of a building. clash: a place where two parts of a building try to occupy the same space, such as a pipe through a beam. walkthrough: walking through a virtual building, room by room, to see it as it will be. mock-up: one room of a building built full-size in virtual space, for real users to try. take-off: measuring the quantities of a building from its model, such as the area of walls and the number of windows.

demo.code:
import hashlib
figures = {"buildings": 5, "squares": 2, "streets": 3, "walks": 6}
keys = sorted(figures)
total_a = sum(figures[k] for k in keys)
total_b = 0
for k in keys:
    total_b += figures[k]
d1 = hashlib.sha256(str(total_a).encode()).hexdigest()
d2 = hashlib.sha256(str(total_b).encode()).hexdigest()
print("total=" + str(total_a))
print("digest_a=" + d1)
print("digest_b=" + d2)
print("match=" + str(d1 == d2))
